Class CachedSqlQuery<B>

java.lang.Object
iu.dao.CachedSqlQuery<B>
Type Parameters:
B - materialized row type
All Implemented Interfaces:
edu.iu.dao.ParameterizedSql, edu.iu.dao.SqlQuery<B>, AutoCloseable
final class CachedSqlQuery<B> extends Object implements edu.iu.dao.SqlQuery<B>
A SqlQuery that reads its cursor once, into a list, and answers every accessor from it.

What draining buys, and what it costs

The delegate is read to exhaustion on the first accessor that returns rows, and the rows are handed to a publisher so that a query can populate the process-wide cache with the individual rows it read. That is the point of this class: one query answers many later loads.

The cost is that getResults(int) is no longer lazy. It still pages — each call returns the next maxRows rows and leaves the cursor where it stopped — but the rows behind those pages have already been materialized, so paging bounds what the caller handles at once rather than what the query holds. A query over a result set too large to hold in memory should not be wrapped.

Cursor semantics

The cursor is honored as SqlQuery describes it. Accessors read forward from the current position; getSingleResult(), getFirstRecord() and getResults() are terminal and close; getResults(int) leaves the position where it stopped. Closing rewinds to the first row, and because the rows are already held, reopening replays them rather than re-reading the database — which is what makes this a cache and not merely a buffer.

getResultSet() is the one accessor a list cannot answer, since it hands the caller the driver's own cursor. It discards whatever has been drained and returns the delegate's result set, so a later list accessor reads forward from wherever the caller left that cursor.
